title: How many traits a generated person carries, and how common each trait should be
question: For a personality model authored as data rows, how many marked traits should an ordinary generated adult carry, how should that number vary across a population, and what relative prevalence should each family of traits have so that a town of a few hundred people reads as a real population rather than as a uniform draw?
whyItMatters: Every generated person currently gets a value on all five shipped traits from the same seeded spread, so nobody is unmarked and nobody is distinctive; five poles is also the entire vocabulary, against a 121-entry catalogue waiting to be authored. Until the count and the prevalence are settled, widening the vocabulary makes the uniformity worse rather than better, because each new row is drawn for everybody on the same curve.
usableAnswer: A distribution for the number of marked traits per adult, stated as a curve or a table rather than a single number; a prevalence band for each of the catalogue's 14 families; a statement of which traits should be rare enough that a player meets one a few times in a lifetime; and the precedent or observation each figure is drawn from.

sourcesChecked.source: Personality_Research_Catalogue.xlsx and Personality_Research_and_Catalogue.md, read in full by the transcripts lane 2026-09-22
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Supplies 121 candidate traits in 14 families with meanings, examples and boundaries, and explicitly declines prevalence, weights and a per-person trait count. The catalogue says those are the owner's to set.
Establishes the five shipped traits and the -2..+2 value scale. It sets no count, because every person carries all five.

Shows the one prevalence curve in use, [-2,-1,-1,0,0,0,0,1,1,2], applied identically to every trait and every person. Nothing recorded says why that shape was chosen or whether it should differ per trait.

sourcesChecked.source: The owner's own answer in the project chat 2026-09-22, that a person should start with one or two traits
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Gives a starting figure and says in the same breath that it will be adjusted. It does not say how the number varies across a population, and it says nothing about prevalence per family.

sourcesChecked.source: docs/research/requests/ordinary-life-trait-set.json, filed by the people and life lane 2026-09-22
sourcesChecked.whatItDidNotSettle: Asks which dispositions are worth modelling and how large the vocabulary should be before entries stop being distinguishable. It is about the size of the list, and says nothing about how many entries a given person carries or how common any of them should be.

notes: This is a different question from ordinary-life-trait-set, which the people and life lane filed the same day. That one asks how many distinct traits should exist in the vocabulary at all. This one asks how many of them any one person should be marked with, and how common each should be across a town. Either can be answered without the other.
The count and the prevalence are separable. An answer to one alone is worth having and should be sent rather than held.
A trait row is data, not code, so any number here is a pack value a modder can change. The answer sets the shipped default, not a permanent rule.
This does not ask what a trait argues for in a given decision. That mapping is authored per decision and is the personality lane's work, not research.
